children.text: The Turumba Festival is an Our Lady of Sorrows devotion held over several months around Easter in Pakil, Laguna. After the prayers of each of the seven Lupi, a procession carrying the image dances through the streets to drums and hymns.

The Turumba Festival is a Catholic festival held in several rounds around Easter in Pakil, Laguna. It honors the image of Our Lady of Sorrows enshrined in Saint Peter of Alcántara Parish Church in Pakil, which locals call Nuestra Señora de los Dolores de Turumba or Mahal na Ina ng Hapis ng Turumba. According to published guides, pilgrims also come from Laguna, Quezon and neighboring provinces. Pakil is a small town on the eastern shore of Laguna de Bay, a quiet town set between the lake and the hills.

According to the legend, in 1788 fishermen on Laguna de Bay found an image of the Virgin Mary floating on the water. The image grew heavier as they carried it ashore, and people took this as a sign that it wished to be enshrined in Pakil's church. The townspeople who saw it are said to have sung, danced and cheered with joy, which is how the festival began. The image of Mary with a pierced heart is explained as a symbol of compassion, suffering and devotion. The name Turumba is said to come from the Tagalog phrase "natumba sa laki ng tuwa" (fell down in great joy).

The backbone of the festival is the seven Lupi. Each Lupi consists of a novena honoring one of the Seven Sorrows of Mary, followed by a procession. The published schedule is the Friday before Palm Sunday, Easter Tuesday, the second Wednesday after Easter, the third Friday after Easter, the fourth Sunday after Easter, the fifth Sunday after Easter or Ascension, and Pentecost Sunday. In some years it coincides with the town fiesta on May 12. In 2026 there was a report that the faithful gathered on Wednesday, April 15. To work out dates yourself, count through the order above from Easter Sunday of that year. For example, in 2026 Easter fell on April 5, so the second Wednesday after Easter was April 15. This calculation is only to help you understand the guide, so confirm the real schedule from parish notices.

The most striking scene comes after each Lupi, when the faithful carry the image out into the streets in a procession. To drums and hymns, the faithful dance and walk in front of the image, and this dance is also called turumba. The atmosphere is far more devout and quiet than a big city festival, so visit with respect for the fact that this is a ritual of the faithful, not a spectacle. Dates change each year with Easter, so you need to check the latest notices from the Pakil municipal government or the parish. The number of visitors in the town jumps during events, and the scene changes greatly from its quiet everyday state. The seven Lupi are spread over several weeks, so for travelers it is convenient that if you miss one, you can aim for the next.

Seven rounds of prayer and procession honoring Our Lady of Sorrows. Dates are set each year based on Easter, so decide which Lupi you want to see and confirm the date before you go. You do not need to attend every Lupi; even one or two will give you the atmosphere. A Lupi that falls on a weekday is hard for working people, so pick one that matches the days you can visit in advance.

After each Lupi, the faithful carry the image and march through the streets, dancing to drums and hymns. The people in the procession express joy and petition with their movements. If you take photos, first read the mood around you and ask permission.

blocks.title: Saint Peter of Alcántara Parish Church

children.text: The parish church of Pakil that houses the image. It is described as a building dating to the 17th century. On days without events it is relatively quiet, so take a slow look inside the church and in front of it.

The setting of the legend in which fishermen pulled the image of Mary from the lake is Laguna de Bay. Seeing the lakeside scenery too helps you understand the background of the festival. Check on site how to get to the lakeshore.

At event times the faithful come on pilgrimage not only from Laguna but also from Quezon and neighboring provinces. Temporary stalls and souvenirs may appear for pilgrims, but their scale and kinds differ every year.
Pakil's town fiesta is on May 12, and in some years it coincides with the novena schedule. In those years the events grow larger.

A late-August 2026 report said Pakil planned its first Turumba-themed film festival for September 3. It is a new attempt to introduce faith and heritage on screen; the venue and program were not yet announced then, and I could not confirm that it took place. The schedule may change from year to year.

blocks.title: A quiet stroll through a Laguna faith town

children.text: Even on days without events, Pakil is a quiet town close to the lake and hills. Some people combine it with a woodcarving town such as nearby Paete. Check the distance on site.

items.title: Day-trip course
items.subtitle: From morning Mass to the afternoon procession

children.text: Set out from Manila toward Laguna. Roads are congested on event days, so an early start is safer.
Arrive in Pakil and look around Saint Peter of Alcántara Parish Church.
Quietly watch the prayers (novena) and Mass held inside the church. The schedule differs each year, so check the notices on site.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town.
Watch the procession pass along its route, which starts in the afternoon.
When the event ends, head back slowly, avoiding the crowds going home.

This is a ritual of the faithful, so avoid overly casual clothing such as shorts or tank tops and keep your voice low. When the procession starts, stand to one side of the road, and when the faithful pass in front, it is better to watch quietly than to take photos. During the strong sun hours, rest in the shade of the church or in a restaurant to save your energy.

items.title: 2 days, 1 night
items.subtitle: Arrive the day before and attend the morning prayers

children.text: Arrive in Pakil or a nearby town the day before the event and drop your bags at your lodging.
Walk through the town around dusk and see the preparations for the event.
Attend the early morning prayers the next day.
Watch the afternoon procession and then head home.
During event weeks, lodging in nearby towns fills up quickly too, so book early.
You can get from Manila to Pakil by bus or van, following the eastern shore of Laguna de Bay. Travel time and fares vary greatly with traffic, so check at the terminal and on site.
On festival days roads are congested and entry to the town may be controlled, so leave extra time.
Parking in town is difficult on event days for cars and rental cars. A realistic plan is to park on the outskirts and walk in.
Same-day tours from Manila sometimes appear. Contents and prices differ by operator.
In town, get around by tricycle or on foot. Fares depend on distance and negotiation.
Roads along the procession route are temporarily closed, so follow the instructions.

The Turumba Festival runs over about three months around Easter. The first Lupi is on the Friday before Palm Sunday and the last is on Pentecost Sunday, so the dates change every year. In 2019 a schedule of April 28 to May 1 was published, and in 2026 there was a report that the faithful gathered on April 15.

Just as the 2020 events were canceled over fears of the spread of COVID, the schedule can change with circumstances. Check the notices from the Pakil municipal government or the parish before you go. April and May are very hot and dry, so bring a hat and water. It is a season of high temperatures and strong sun, so do not stand outdoors for long at daytime events, and build rest time in the shade of the church into your plan.

If you want to see Pakil at its calmest, a weekday walk through the church and lake town on a day without a Lupi is also good. You will not see the festival procession, but you can calmly take in the church architecture and everyday life in the town.

Pakil has few places to stay, so many people stay in nearby towns or toward Pagsanjan. Rooms fill up quickly during event weeks, so book early. Facilities and rates differ by property, so check recent reviews. Outside event weeks, a day trip without an overnight stay is quite enough.

At restaurants and stalls in town you can try Filipino home cooking and snacks. As a lake town, freshwater fish dishes may also appear, but menus differ by restaurant. At pilgrimage events, stalls may appear where the faithful gather, so check hygiene before you eat.

If you are making a same-day trip from Manila, it is better to eat lunch before the procession starts. Once the procession begins, roads get blocked and restaurants get crowded. Restaurants in town are small, so groups should claim a table early. It helps to carry water and light snacks in your bag.
Check the Pakil municipal government and parish notices first, since dates change with Easter.
This is a religious ritual of the faithful. Dress modestly and keep your voice low.
When taking photos, ask permission before close-ups of people's faces in the procession.
April and May are very hot, so be sure to bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
The procession route is crowded, so go early and claim a spot.
Bring cash. Market stalls and tricycles are generally cash.
Avoid flash inside the church and avoid photographing during Mass.
Watch for pickpockets on event days and keep your belongings in front of you. The elderly should avoid standing for long in the crowd along the procession route.
Phone batteries drain fast on event days, so bring a power bank.
This is a religious event, its dates change every year, and April and May are very hot.
Watch for heatstroke and dehydration, and drink water often.
Roads along the procession may be controlled, so follow the instructions.

Do not cut into the faithful's dance or block the way during the procession.
